labels: How do we store these data sets

title: Motivating Example
summary: Motivates the need for arrays by showing how storing grades for many students using individual variables becomes impractical.
main_text: Suppose I need to store the grades for all students so I can then compute statistics, sort them, print them, etc. I would need to store them in variables that I could access and use. This is easy if I have 3 or 4 students. This is painful if I have many students. Code example 1: int main() { int score1, score2, score3; cin >> score1 >> score2 >> score3; // output scores in sorted order if(score1 < score2 && score1 < score3) { /* score 1 is smallest */ } /* more */ }. Code example 2: int main() { int score1, score2, score3, score4, score5, score6, score7, score8, score9, score10, score11, score12, score13, score14, score15, /* ... */ score139, score140; cin >> score1 >> score2 >> score3 >> score4 >> score5 >> score6 /* ... */ }.
notes_text: This motivating example shows why we need a better data structure than individual variables when dealing with many related values of the same type.

title: Control vs. Data Structures
summary: Distinguishes control structures (if, while, for) from data structures, introducing arrays as C/C++'s native data structure.
main_text: Language constructs that allow us to make decisions are referred to as control structures. The common ones are: if statements, while loops, for loops. We also need ways to store our data so we can access it easily and efficiently. Arrays are the simplest data structure and the only one that C/C++ supports natively. Other data structures are available through other library code (but arrays need no additional code included).
notes_text: This slide draws an important distinction between control flow and data organization, setting up the conceptual framework for understanding why arrays are fundamental.

title: Array Basics
summary: Defines arrays as named, ordered, same-type collections accessed by index and stored contiguously in memory, with declaration and loop-based input examples.
main_text: An array is a named collection of ordered variables of the same type that are accessed with an index and stored contiguously in memory. Named collection: One name to refer to the collection of variables. Ordered: There is a first and a last and one comes before another. Accessed with an index: Each variable is accessed with its position/index (using [] brackets). Same Type: Variables in one array must all be the same type (one array can't store doubles and ints). Code example: int main() { int scores[140]; // allocates 140 integers // with garbage values for(int i=0; i < 140; i++){ cin >> scores[i]; } } Once allocated, we can only access 1 element at a time via its index.
notes_text: Key concept: array indexing starts at 0. The memory diagram shows addresses 520, 524, 528 etc. with indices [0], [1], [2] and values 96, 84, 93, ..., 90.

images.description: Memory diagram showing an array called 'scores' stored contiguously in memory with addresses 520, 524, 528, ..., 1076, indices [0], [1], [2], ..., [139], and sample values 96, 84, 93, ..., 90.

title: Accessing An Element
summary: Explains how to access individual array elements using any expression as an index, with examples of constants, variables, and arithmetic expressions.
main_text: Once an array is declared, there is nothing "special" about it. Each variable must be initialized and accessed 1 at a time. To access an individual variable/element of an array of size n, use the name of the array followed by square brackets containing ANY expression (constant, variable, arithmetic) that will evaluate to an index from 0 to n-1. Note: Indexing starts at 0. Code example: int main() { int x = 1, myval = 5; int scores[10]; // allocates 10 integers scores[4] = 73; scores[x] = 82; // sets scores[1] scores[2*x + 1] = 93; // sets scores[3] scores[1+max(x,myval)] = 88; // sets scores[6] }. The key is you can generate the index of the desired element using any legal C++ code that will result in the desired index.
notes_text: The memory diagram shows addresses 520-544 with indices [0]-[6], values ??, 82, ??, 93, 73, ??, 88 after the assignments.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the scores array after various assignments, with addresses 520-544, indices [0]-[6], and values ??, 82, ??, 93, 73, ??, 88 demonstrating how different index expressions map to memory locations.

title: Index vs. Value
summary: Clarifies the distinction between an array index (the expression in brackets) and the value/data stored at that index, with a practice exercise.
main_text: The expression in the square brackets is an index. Using array[index] yields the data/value in the array at that index. An index can be ANY EXPRESSION, even the value from an array or the return value from a function. For an array declared to be size n, only indices 0 to n-1 are legal. Code example: int main() { int scores[20]; /* ... fill in the data ... */ int i = 1; int x = scores[2*i + 1]; // x=_ int y = scores[ scores[1] ]; // y=_ int z = scores[max(4,2)]; // z=_ return 0; }. The diagram shows scores[2*i+1] where the bracket portion is the index and the entire expression yields the Value/data.
notes_text: Memory diagram shows scores with indices [0]-[4] having values 9, 0, 7, 8, 6. This is the exercise version with blanks for students to fill in.

images.description: Annotated diagram showing scores[2*i+1] with braces indicating that '2*i+1' is the index portion and the whole expression yields the Value/data.

title: Loops and Arrays (1)
summary: Demonstrates combining loops with arrays, using the loop variable as the array index to initialize or read all elements efficiently.
main_text: The real power of arrays is found when you combine them with loops. Use the loop control variable (int i) to serve as the index of the array entry to be modified or accessed. Whether the array has 1 or 1,000,000 elements, our code size does not grow. Code example: int main() { int x = 1, myval = 5; int scores[100]; // allocates 100 integers // initialize all to 0 for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ scores[i] = 0; } // ..OR.. read in all entries for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ cin >> scores[i]; } }
notes_text: Memory diagram shows all elements initialized to 0 at addresses 520-540 with indices [0]-[6].

title: When Do We Need Arrays?
summary: Explains that arrays are needed only when data must be revisited, and that simple tasks like averages can be computed without storing all data.
main_text: Arrays can store many related data items of the same type. A better question is when do we need to store these related data items in an array? We need arrays when we need to revisit the data more than once. If we just want to find the min/max or average we could just get the data from the user and update the sum or min/max as we go and not need to store each data item. Don't introduce arrays where they are not needed. Code example with array (two passes): int main() { int scores[100]; // Get the data for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ cin >> scores[i]; } // Average all values int sum = 0; for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ sum += scores[i]; } cout << sum / 100.0 << endl; return 0; }. Code example without array (single pass): int main() { int val, sum = 0; // Get the data & average it // at the same time for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ cin >> val; sum += val; } cout << sum / 100.0 << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: This is an important design principle: only use arrays when you truly need to revisit data. The single-pass approach is more memory-efficient when you don't need to keep the data around.

title: A Common Error - Out-of-Bounds Access
summary: Warns about out-of-bounds array access errors that cause data corruption or segmentation faults, with examples of incorrect and safe code.
main_text: Care must be taken to ensure no index is used that will lead to an out-of-bounds access. Such an access will either corrupt other data or cause the program to crash! These are often known as segmentation faults. When you see one, your first thought should be to check for a bad array index! Code example: int main() { int scores[20]; /* ... init in the data ... */ int i; for(i=0; i <= 20; i++){ // wrong? scores[i] = 0; } cin >> i; // what could happen here..not safe scores[i] = 100; // safe if( i >= 0 && i < 20 ){ scores[i] = 100; } return 0; }
notes_text: The off-by-one error (using <= instead of <) is one of the most common bugs. The memory diagram shows index [19] as the last valid element, with index 20 (address 600) being out of bounds and marked with '?'.

images.description: Memory diagram showing scores array with indices [0]-[19] at addresses 520-596, with an out-of-bounds access at address 600 marked with '?' to illustrate the danger of accessing beyond array bounds.

title: Important C/C++ Rule: Array Size
summary: Explains that C/C++ requires array sizes to be known at compile time, and the course workaround of allocating a large fixed-size array.
main_text: C/C++ needs to know the SIZE of the array when the program is compiled, not when it is run. This implies the size of the array must be ONE, FIXED (or constant) size everytime the program is run. For this course, we will just allocate a LARGE array of the maximum size potentially needed and then use only a portion of it as the program runs. Future courses will teach you how to deal with this correctly and not waste array space. Code example (good): int main() { // GOOD!! int data[24]; // 24 known at compile time // BAD!! int n; cin >> n; int data[n]; // n not known at compile time }. Code example (course approach): int main() { int data[100]; // max needed int n; cin >> n; for(int i=0; i < n; i++) { cin >> data[i]; } }
notes_text: Variable-length arrays (VLAs) are not standard C++ and should be avoided. The pattern of allocating a max-size array and tracking the actual used size with a separate variable is the standard approach for this course.

title: Initializing Arrays With Constants
summary: Shows how to initialize arrays with constant values using initialization lists, including partial initialization and compiler-inferred sizing.
main_text: Arrays can be initialized with constants when they are declared. To do so, use an initialization list which is a comma separated list of constants in {...}. Exception: If fewer values are provided than the size of the array, remaining elements will be filled with 0s. If an initialization list is provided you need not specify the size in the square brackets (i.e. just use empty []) as the compiler can figure out what size the array must be by counting the initial values. Code examples: int main() { int data[5] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; double dec[4] = {0.25, 0.3}; // dec = {0.25, 0.3, 0, 0} int nums[4] = {0}; // nums = {0, 0, 0, 0} } int main() { int data[] = {9, 7, 8, 9, 5}; // allocates array of size 5 double dec[] = {0.25, 0.3, 0.18, 0.2}; // allocates array of size 4 }
notes_text: The {0} idiom is a convenient way to zero-initialize an entire array. Specifying sizes is not necessary when using initial values list.

title: Sequential vs. Random Access
summary: Distinguishes sequential access (looping through all elements) from random access (computing a single index), with examples of each pattern.
main_text: Most array-based tasks fall into either a sequential-access pattern or random-access pattern. Sequential access iterates (loops) through all elements. Used for tasks that require looking at all elements in the worst case. Random access computes the ONE index to access. Used for tasks that only require accessing one specific element. Sequential access example: int total = 0; for(int i=0; i < 20; i++){ total += scores[i]; }. Random access example: int stuID; cout << "Enter ID\n"; cin >> stuId; cout << "Your score: "; cout << scores[stuId]; cout << endl;
notes_text: The diagrams show sequential access as a horizontal arrow traversing the entire array, and random access as a single arrow pointing directly to one element (index [2]) based on a stuID value of 2.

images.description: Two memory diagrams contrasting access patterns. Top: sequential access shown with a long horizontal arrow spanning all elements from index [0] to [19]. Bottom: random access shown with stuID=2 pointing directly to index [2] containing value 93.

title: Sequential Access Tasks
summary: Lists common tasks requiring sequential access: combining all elements (sum, average, count-if, modify-all) and searching/selecting elements.
main_text: To repeat: Use sequential access when you MUST (or POTENTIALLY need to) visit EVERY element. Common tasks that require sequential access: Combining ALL elements: Sum or average, Count-if (e.g. count how many 100s), Modify-all (e.g. increment all). Search / select an element potentially stopping (break) early (in an unsorted array): Find a particular value, Minimum / maximum.
notes_text: Two diagrams illustrate: (1) a sum/average traversal with a horizontal arrow across all elements feeding into a 'sum' accumulator, and (2) a find(96) search traversal scanning from left to right.

images.description: Two memory diagrams: top shows sequential traversal with arrow across all elements and accumulator variable 'sum'; bottom shows find(96) search scanning from index [0] rightward through the array.

title: Loops and Arrays (2) - Average Score Solution
summary: Provides the complete solution for computing the average score using a loop to sum array elements and finding the maximum value.
main_text: How could we determine the average score? Solution code: int main() { int scores[100]; /* ... fill in the data ... */ // Average all values int sum = 0; for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ sum += scores[i]; } cout << (double)sum / 100 << endl; // Find maximum int max = 0; for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ if( scores[i] > max) max = scores[i]; } cout << "Max: " << max << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: This is the solution to the exercise from slide 9. The average uses an int sum variable accumulated in a loop, then cast to double for the division. The max-finding loop is also included here. Memory diagram shows scores with values 9, 7, 8, 8, 6.

images.description: Memory diagram showing scores array with values 9, 7, 8, 8, 6 at indices [0]-[4], addresses 520-536.

title: Loops and Arrays (3) - Maximum Score Solution
summary: Provides the complete solution for finding the maximum value in an array, initializing max to -1 and updating when a larger element is found.
main_text: How could we determine the max score? Solution code: int main() { int scores[100]; /* ... fill in the data ... */ // Find maximum int max = -1; for(int i=0; i < 100; i++){ if( scores[i] > max) max = scores[i]; } cout << "Max: " << max << endl; return 0; }
notes_text: This is the solution to the exercise from slide 10. The max variable is initialized to -1 (assuming scores are non-negative). Memory diagram shows scores with values 9, 7, 8, 8, 6.

title: Index vs. Value - Solution
summary: Provides the solved version of the index vs. value exercise, showing computed values x=8, y=9, z=6 from array expressions.
main_text: The expression in the square brackets is an index. Using array[index] yields the data/value in the array at that index. An index can be ANY EXPRESSION, even the value from an array or the return value from a function. For an array declared to be size n, only indices 0 to n-1 are legal. Solution code: int main() { int scores[20]; /* ... fill in the data ... */ int i = 1; int x = scores[2*i + 1]; // x=8 int y = scores[ scores[1] ]; // y=9 int z = scores[max(4,2)]; // z=6 return 0; }. Explanation: scores[2*1+1] = scores[3] = 8. scores[scores[1]] = scores[0] = 9. scores[max(4,2)] = scores[4] = 6.
notes_text: This is the solution to the exercise from slide 7. Memory diagram shows scores with indices [0]-[4] having values 9, 0, 7, 8, 6. The nested index scores[scores[1]] evaluates scores[1]=0, then scores[0]=9.
